_readme: EVENTLOOP-PROBE — resolves a CONTRADICTION between theory (better-sqlite3 is a
synchronous API; a blocked write should freeze the whole process) and a prior
measurement (E7-round-2's eventloop_freeze_probe, eval/e7-round2.json, which
reported 'not frozen': a concurrent read returned in 29ms while a write was mid a
5.26s busy_timeout wait). MEASUREMENT ONLY per the task brief — nothing under
src/ was touched; a concurrent agent (F13) was editing src/mcp/staleness.ts
throughout this session (see build_state below for exactly what was built).
Pre-committed interpretation, written BEFORE running anything (per the task
brief's explicit instruction to record this first):
- If Phase 1 shows a freeze (timer gap ~= block duration): BEGIN IMMEDIATE +
busy_timeout is NOT viable as F11's sole mechanism for in-process writes;
writes must move off the main thread or coordination must stay async/
app-level. Report that plainly.
- If Phase 1 shows no freeze: explain WHY the synchronous-API reasoning is
wrong before anyone builds on it — a result contradicting a clear mechanism
needs an explanation, not just a number.
RESULT: Phase 1 shows an unambiguous, total freeze in both directions tested
(success-after-wait and timeout). The synchronous-API reasoning was RIGHT.
The prior 'not frozen' measurement was an artifact — see phase_2 below for
exactly what the artifact was, verified by tracing the actual write-path code
(not just re-running the same black-box probe).
Method (build up from the primitive, per the task brief):
Phase 1 — isolate the primitive, NO mast code at all: two plain better-sqlite3
connections, a lock holder (process A) and a writer that arms an
independent event-loop liveness probe (setInterval heartbeat +
perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay) BEFORE attempting a write that must wait
on A's held BEGIN IMMEDIATE. This is the decisive result.
Phase 2 — confirm in the real system: a real `mast serve` process driven over
stdio, with a raw second better-sqlite3 connection bypassing
structure.lock to force the real write path onto the SQLite busy_timeout
path, PLUS a series of read-only probe calls sent throughout the hold
window (not one sample) so genuine overlap is verified from logged
timestamps, not assumed.
Phase 3 (+ explains Phase 2's anomaly) — an isolated mechanism test using
dist/graph/db.js's real openDatabase (Kysely) against a raw competing
connection, comparing three transaction shapes side by side: Kysely's
actual deferred-BEGIN read-then-write shape vs. a holding-only competitor,
the same shape vs. a committing competitor (the original busy_snapshot_repro
scenario), and the SAME query shape wrapped in an explicit BEGIN IMMEDIATE
instead of Kysely's deferred BEGIN.
Harness (kept OUTSIDE this package, /Users/spikedpunchvictim/temp/mast-bench/,
per the task's measurement-only scope — nothing here is shipped):
phase1-lock-holder.mjs         Process A: opens a bare sqlite file (no mast
code), BEGIN IMMEDIATE, holds for holdMs,
commits. Prints LOCKED/RELEASED markers.
phase1-writer-probe.mjs        Process B (the process under test): arms a
50ms setInterval heartbeat AND
perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay BEFORE
attempting BEGIN IMMEDIATE against the SAME
file A already holds. Reports heartbeat gaps
and event-loop-delay histogram stats.
phase1-run.mjs                 Orchestrator: spawns A, waits for its LOCKED
marker, then spawns B, combines both
processes' output into one JSON result.
phase2-realserver-probe.mjs    Real `mast serve --no-startup-reindex` driven
over stdio; a raw second better-sqlite3
connection (bypassing structure.lock) holds
BEGIN IMMEDIATE on graph.db with a 1500ms
head start (vs the earlier e7r2 probe's
200ms) before the target file is touched and
the write-triggering tool call is sent. A
SERIES of read-only mast_signature probes
(500ms cadence) is sent for the whole hold
window, each logged sentAt/resolvedAt plus
whether the write was still outstanding at
send/resolve time — this is what verifies
genuine overlap instead of assuming it from
one sample.
phase3-busy-mechanism.mjs      Three side-by-side scenarios against
dist/graph/db.js's real openDatabase: (1)
Kysely deferred-BEGIN read-then-write vs a
competitor that only HOLDS BEGIN IMMEDIATE
(never writes) — this is what Phase 2's raw
probe actually does; (2) the same shape vs a
competitor that COMMITS a real write mid-
transaction (the original busy_snapshot_repro
scenario, re-confirmed here); (3) the SAME
read-then-write SQL wrapped in a raw BEGIN
IMMEDIATE instead of Kysely's deferred BEGIN,
against a competitor running in a SEPARATE OS
process (an earlier same-process version of
this scenario self-deadlocked — see
methodology_notes.same_process_self_deadlock).
To regenerate:
1. pnpm -F mast build   (record `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git status --short
src/` alongside the run — see build_state; a concurrent agent may have
changed src/ by the time this is re-run).
2. Phase 1 needs NO mast state at all:
node phase1-run.mjs case_a_success <dbpath> 2000 5000 50 <outFile>   (x2+ reps)
node phase1-run.mjs case_b_timeout  <dbpath> 8000 3000 50 <outFile>   (x2+ reps)
3. Fresh state dir, sibling of nest (NOT mast-state/baseline-state/f1-state/
m1-*-sqlite/e7-state/e7r2-state/audit2):
mast init nest --state-dir <abs>/eventloop-probe-state --no-index
mast index nest --state-dir <abs>/eventloop-probe-state --phase1-only
4. node phase2-realserver-probe.mjs <abs>/eventloop-probe-state <abs nest> 7000 <outFile>
node phase2-realserver-probe.mjs <abs>/eventloop-probe-state <abs nest> 4000 <outFile>
5. cp -r eventloop-probe-state eventloop-probe-state-phase3X   (fresh copy per
rep — scenario 1/2 mutate/roll back rows, scenario 3 leaves a real commit)

build_state.note: A concurrent agent (F13) was actively editing src/mcp/staleness.ts for this whole session, per this task's own scope note. `pnpm build` was run ONCE at the start of this probe (clean tsc, no errors) to produce a working dist/ for Phase 2/3; the built dist/mcp/staleness.js already includes F13's fix (retry populateFile once, without sleep, for SQLITE_BUSY/SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT specifically, falling back to {busy:true} on exhaustion rather than throwing) — confirmed by reading src/mcp/staleness.ts's isRetryableBusySnapshot/MAX_POPULATE_RETRIES directly, not inferred. This F13 fix materially affects Phase 2's result (see phase_2.explanation_of_earlier_no_freeze_artifact) — Phase 1 and Phase 3 do not depend on it (Phase 1 uses no mast code; Phase 3 exercises the underlying SQLite/Kysely mechanism directly, independent of staleness.ts's retry policy).

phase_1_primitive_verdict.headline: FROZEN — unambiguous, in both directions tested. A blocked better-sqlite3 write (busy_timeout retry, native synchronous call) stops the ENTIRE calling process's event loop for the full duration of the block: not one heartbeat fires, and perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay records a single delay sample equal to the block. This is the decisive result the task brief specified — the theory was right.

case_a_success_after_wait.setup: Process A: BEGIN IMMEDIATE, holds 2000ms, commits. Process B (under test): arms a 50ms heartbeat + monitorEventLoopDelay, THEN attempts its own BEGIN IMMEDIATE against the same file. Since B's busy_timeout (5000ms) exceeds A's hold (2000ms), B's write should succeed after waiting.
case_a_success_after_wait.reading: maxHeartbeatGapMs and eventLoopDelayMaxMs both track blockedMs almost exactly (rep2: 1602ms block, 1651ms gap, 1606ms max delay) — the ~50-100ms slack is the heartbeat interval's own granularity plus scheduling jitter on either side of the block, not evidence against a total freeze. Every other heartbeat (before and after the block) landed within a few ms of its 50ms schedule; only the ONE spanning the block was anomalous, and it fully accounts for the block.

case_b_timeout.setup: Process A: BEGIN IMMEDIATE, holds 8000ms. Process B: busy_timeout = 3000ms (deliberately shorter than A's hold), so B's write must genuinely exhaust its busy_timeout and throw.
case_b_timeout.reading: Identical pattern to case (a): the process freezes for exactly as long as busy_timeout has been configured to retry, REGARDLESS of whether the retry ultimately succeeds or exhausts and throws. Freezing is a property of the retry loop itself (native, synchronous, no yield points), not of the outcome.

phase_2_real_system.setup: Real `mast serve --no-startup-reindex` against a fresh phase1-indexed nest corpus. A raw second better-sqlite3 connection (bypassing structure.lock entirely, exactly as the earlier e7r2 probe did) holds `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on graph.db, with a 1500ms head start (vs the earlier probe's 200ms) before the target file is touched and the write-triggering `mast_signature` call is sent. A SERIES of read-only `mast_signature` probes (different, untouched file/symbol — fast stat-only path) is sent at 500ms intervals for the entire hold window, each timestamped sentAt/resolvedAt with an explicit `writeOutstandingAtSend`/`writeOutstandingAtResolve` flag so overlap is verified from the data, not assumed.

write_call.result: valid JSON, results: [] (no error, no busy flag visible in the response body)
valid JSON, results: [] (no error, no busy flag visible in the response body)

phase_2_real_system.headline_finding: In BOTH runs the write resolved in well under 700ms — nowhere near the 5000ms busy_timeout the connection is configured with — DESPITE the raw competitor holding its lock for the entire 5.2-8.9s window. No genuine multi-second block ever formed to test freezing against; every read probe returned in tens of ms because there was nothing blocking the process at the time. This directly reproduces the earlier e7r2 probe's dominant pattern (5 of its 6 runs also failed near-instantly) and explains it precisely — see explanation_of_earlier_no_freeze_artifact below, verified against the actual write-path code, not re-guessed from the black-box timing alone.

explanation_of_earlier_no_freeze_artifac.root_cause: populateFile (src/graph/populate.ts:102) wraps its writes in Kysely's `.transaction().execute()`, which issues a DEFERRED `BEGIN` (Kysely's sqlite-driver.js:32-34) — the transaction's first statement is a READ (F12's monotonic-guard SELECT). Phase 3's isolated test (scenario 1, below) proves that when this exact read-then-write shape runs against ANY competing connection that already holds `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` — even one that never writes anything, just holds the reservation — SQLite returns plain `SQLITE_BUSY` in 1-2ms. It does NOT invoke the busy-handler / busy_timeout retry loop at all. This is a structural property of promoting an open read transaction to a write transaction while another writer already holds the reservation, not a time-dependent retry that merely happened to be fast.
explanation_of_earlier_no_freeze_artifac.why_this_makes_the_earlier_run_1_anomalo: The earlier probe's ONE run that DID show a genuine ~5.26s block (its strongest 'not frozen' evidence — a 29ms concurrent read while the write was still pending) used only a 200ms head start before touching the target file, versus this probe's 1500ms. The most likely explanation, consistent with everything measured here: with a short head start there is a real chance A's read (the first statement of its deferred transaction) executes in a narrow window BEFORE B's BEGIN IMMEDIATE has fully landed — meaning A's transaction does NOT begin as an 'open read being promoted while a writer already holds the reservation' (the structural instant-BUSY case Phase 3 reproduces), but instead only meets B's lock later, at write time, as ordinary ab-initio lock contention — which DOES engage the standard busy-handler/busy_timeout retry. Under that reading, the earlier probe's one 5.26s run genuinely entered the synchronous busy-wait Phase 1 tested — and Phase 1 proves that state is IMPOSSIBLE to service a concurrent read from in the same process. The earlier probe's read call was sent 1500ms after the write and returned in 29ms; if the write was truly inside its synchronous block at that point (extremely likely, since JIT parse+populateFile setup takes ~10-20ms per eval/e7-round2.json's own hold-decomposition data, nowhere near 1500ms), a 29ms concurrent response is a direct contradiction of Phase 1's mechanism. This was not independently re-run with the exact original probe's 200ms-head-start timing to catch the artifact live (today's F13-fixed code makes reproducing that specific race far harder — see below) — this is the best-supported explanation from the evidence available, stated as inference, not re-confirmed at that exact race window.
explanation_of_earlier_no_freeze_artifac.an_independent_confound_this_probe_also_: src/mcp/staleness.ts's F13 fix (isRetryableBusySnapshot, staleness.ts:36-38) retries populateFile once, WITHOUT sleeping, for BOTH SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT and plain SQLITE_BUSY — explicitly reasoned in its own WHY-comment as covering ordinary SQLITE_BUSY 'for free' because a stale snapshot needs a fresh transaction, not time. Combined with the structural instant-BUSY finding above, this means TODAY's actual write path (post-F13) essentially NEVER reaches a genuine busy_timeout wait via the JIT refresh path AT ALL under contention — it fails fast (both attempts, ~1-2ms each at the SQL layer) and gracefully degrades to {busy:true}, which — per the same code trace done for this probe — has no home in mast_signature's response body when the requested symbol's query comes back empty (signature.ts:52-108: topLevelBusy is only attached per-result inside the results loop; an empty result set silently discards it). That gap is a genuine, separately-reportable defect (see new_defect_found below) but is NOT this probe's confound: the fast-fail timing itself (1-2ms) is a property of the SQL transaction SHAPE (Phase 3 scenario 1, using the SAME dist/graph/db.js Kysely config independent of staleness.ts's retry policy), not of F13's retry logic, which only decides what happens AFTER the fast failure.

phase_2_real_system.new_defect_found_not_fixed: mast_signature's response has no top-level busy/stale field. When the JIT refresh returns {busy:true} (write path blocked/failing) for a file whose requested symbol query comes back with zero results, `topLevelBusy` (signature.ts) is computed correctly but is only ever attached inside the per-result loop (line ~107) — with zero results, that loop body never runs, so the busy signal is silently discarded. The caller receives a clean-looking `{results: [], _stats: {...}}` with no indication the file may be stale. This reproduces (a variant of) the NEW_DEFECT already flagged in eval/e7-round2.json's busy_snapshot_repro section, and confirms it is UNCHANGED by F13's otherwise-correct fix to the per-result busy flag — F13 fixed the throw, not this separate empty-results gap. Reporting per the task brief's instruction; NOT fixed (measurement-only scope).

phase_3_begin_immediate_vs_busy_snapshot.setup: dbA opened via the real dist/graph/db.js openDatabase (same Kysely config the server uses). rawB is a plain better-sqlite3 connection to the same graph.db. Three scenarios run back-to-back against a fresh copy of the state dir per rep, 2 reps.

scenario_1_deferred_read_then_write_vs_h.description: Kysely's actual populateFile shape (SELECT then UPDATE inside one deferred-BEGIN transaction) vs. a raw competitor that ONLY holds BEGIN IMMEDIATE (never writes) — this is exactly what Phase 2's raw probe does against the real server.
scenario_1_deferred_read_then_write_vs_h.reading: Confirms the root cause named in phase_2: this fails in 1-2ms, not via a multi-second busy_timeout retry, EVEN THOUGH nothing about B's state ever changes (no data written, no commit) — the busy-handler is never invoked for this specific 'promote an open read transaction while another connection already holds the write reservation' case.

scenario_2_deferred_read_then_write_vs_c.description: Same deferred-BEGIN shape, but B actually COMMITS a real write to the same table between A's read and A's write — the original eval/e7-round2.json busy_snapshot_repro scenario, re-run here for a direct side-by-side.
scenario_2_deferred_read_then_write_vs_c.reading: Reconfirms the prior 5/5 finding: busy_timeout genuinely does not apply to this error class, and it fires in ~1ms regardless of the connection's busy_timeout pragma.

scenario_3_begin_immediate_guard_vs_hold.description: The SAME read-then-write SQL (SELECT existing mtime, UPDATE) but issued via a raw `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` instead of Kysely's deferred BEGIN — this IS the 'deeper fix' IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md's F11 section already names (staleness.ts:145-148: 'BEGIN IMMEDIATE for the guard transaction... F11 territory'). B (the competitor) runs as a genuinely separate OS process via phase1-lock-holder.mjs, holding for 1200ms then releasing.
scenario_3_begin_immediate_guard_vs_hold.reading: BEGIN IMMEDIATE eliminates BOTH the instant-SQLITE_BUSY failure (scenario 1) AND SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT (scenario 2) — there is no open read transaction to promote or invalidate, since the write lock is taken FIRST. It correctly falls back to the ordinary busy_timeout wait: elapsed time (~1290ms) tracks B's 1200ms hold almost exactly, not an instant failure and not the full 5000ms timeout. This is Phase 3's direct answer: (a) BEGIN IMMEDIATE never produces BUSY_SNAPSHOT — confirmed; (b) it waits on busy_timeout as intended, and that wait is real (bounded by the actual competitor, not always the full timeout) — confirmed.

phase_3_begin_immediate_vs_busy_snapshot.verdict: CONFIRMED both parts of Phase 3's question. This is good news for F11's already-recommended deeper fix (apply BEGIN IMMEDIATE to F12's guard transaction) — it is a genuine correctness improvement over the current deferred-BEGIN shape. But per Phase 1, adopting it means any GENUINE contention on that transaction (not the instant-fail cases it removes, but real busy_timeout waits it now enables) WILL freeze the whole mast-serve process for up to the configured busy_timeout (currently 5000ms, connection-wide) — see f11_recommendation below for why this needs a short, dedicated busy_timeout override, not the shared 5000ms default.

methodology_notes.same_process_self_deadlock: An earlier version of Phase 3's scenario 3 ran B (the lock holder, scheduled to release via a JS setTimeout) in the SAME process as A. A's synchronous `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` call blocked the entire process (per Phase 1), which meant B's own setTimeout-scheduled release callback could never fire while A was blocked — A ended up waiting out its FULL 5000ms busy_timeout and throwing, instead of succeeding after B's intended 1200ms release. This is not a discarded mistake: it is a THIRD, independent, accidental reconfirmation of Phase 1's freeze finding (a same-process timer genuinely could not fire during the block), found by a bug rather than by design. Fixed by running B as a true external OS process (phase1-lock-holder.mjs) for the reported scenario_3 result.
methodology_notes.corpus_drift: Phase 2 touches packages/core/injector/internal-providers-storage.ts (appends a dummy comment) once per run, consistent with eval/e7-round2.json's own documented convention for this harness (not cleaned up afterward, same rationale: the JIT harness only cares about lock/timing behaviour, not file content).
methodology_notes.state_dirs_used: eventloop-probe-state (fresh, phase1-indexed) plus disposable copies eventloop-probe-state-phase3b/-phase3c for Phase 3's reps (scenario 1 rolls back its mutation; scenario 2 and 3 leave real committed rows — hence fresh copies per rep rather than reusing one dir). None of mast-state/baseline-state/f1-state/m1-*-sqlite/e7-state/e7r2-state/audit2 were touched.
methodology_notes.no_src_changes: Confirmed: `git status --short src/` before and after this probe shows only the pre-existing F13-in-progress changes (src/graph/db.ts, src/graph/populate.ts, src/mcp/staleness.ts) already present when this probe started — nothing from this probe's own work modified any file under src/.

f11_recommendation.verdict: The theory was RIGHT, not the prior measurement. Do NOT cite eval/e7-round2.json's eventloop_freeze_probe as evidence that relying on raw SQLite locking (F11 design option (c), 'delete the lock, rely on SQLite') is safe — Phase 1 proves definitively, with direct timer-gap evidence in both the success and timeout directions, that a genuinely-blocked better-sqlite3 call freezes the ENTIRE calling process's event loop, including all unrelated concurrent work, for the full duration of the block. Option (c) remains REFUTED, now on stronger grounds than the plan's original 'verified fact' citation alone.
f11_recommendation.why_todays_system_hasnt_hit_this_yet: Every write path in src/ (grep for `db.transaction()`/`.transaction()`: graph/populate.ts:102,695, store/sqliteChunkStore.ts:56,74) uses Kysely's `.transaction().execute()`, which issues a deferred BEGIN. Phase 3 scenario 1 shows this specific shape fails in 1-2ms under contention (SQLITE_BUSY, structurally, not time-dependent) rather than ever entering a genuine busy_timeout wait — so today's actual code is accidentally safe from the freeze scenario, not because busy-waits don't freeze, but because the current transaction shape almost never reaches one. This is also why Phase 2 could not reproduce a genuine multi-second block against the real server despite trying twice with different hold durations.
f11_recommendation.actionable_implication_for_f11_option_d: IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md's already-recommended option (d) includes 'write-behind, best-effort persist... under a short BEGIN IMMEDIATE... on busy, drop it — costs latency, never correctness.' Phase 1 + Phase 3 together confirm this is the RIGHT shape (BEGIN IMMEDIATE genuinely fixes BUSY_SNAPSHOT, per Phase 3 scenario 3) but sharpen a requirement the plan's prose left implicit: the busy_timeout used for that specific write-behind persist MUST be a SHORT, dedicated override (e.g. 100-300ms), not graph/db.ts's shared connection-wide 5000ms default — because per Phase 1, whatever busy_timeout value is configured is also the MAXIMUM freeze window for the whole process if that specific write genuinely contends. A short timeout bounds the worst case to something an interactive tool call can absorb; the current 5000ms default, if ever actually exercised by a real contending write, would freeze the whole server (all concurrent reads too, not just the one blocked writer) for up to 5 full seconds.
f11_recommendation.actionable_implication_for_f12s_small_fi: Applying BEGIN IMMEDIATE to F12's guard transaction (already floated as the 'deeper fix' at staleness.ts:145-148) is a good, confirmed-working correctness improvement (Phase 3 scenario 3) that should ship — but it should NOT reuse the connection's shared 5000ms busy_timeout unmodified. Structure.lock already serializes essentially all of today's real writers before they ever reach SQLite, so genuine SQL-level contention on this specific transaction should be rare in practice — but 'rare' is not 'never' (the plan's own note that the manifest/index.json phase and any lock-bypassing path are NOT covered by structure.lock), and per Phase 1, whenever it does happen, the freeze window equals whatever busy_timeout is configured for that statement. Recommend a short (100-300ms) override here too, consistent with option (d)'s reasoning, rather than accepting an up-to-5s freeze for what should be a rare, recoverable event under §9.0's TOCTOU policy.
f11_recommendation.structure_lock_stays_primary: Unchanged from the plan's existing verdict: structure.lock remains the primary serialization mechanism for coarse writers (reindex batches, manifest phase, checker-resolver) — it is what prevents real writers from reaching genuine SQLite-level contention with each other in practice today, and per this probe, that is materially load-bearing: it is the reason the freeze scenario Phase 1 proves is real hasn't yet been observed in production-shaped traffic.
f11_recommendation.summary_one_line: Freeze is real (Phase 1, decisive). Today's code is accidentally shielded from it by a transaction shape that fails fast instead of blocking (Phase 2+3). The plan's recommended fixes (BEGIN IMMEDIATE for F12's guard, write-behind under a bounded busy_timeout for option (d)) are correct in shape but need an explicit SHORT busy_timeout override wherever they engage the real retry path, not the shared 5000ms default — otherwise fixing BUSY_SNAPSHOT correctness would trade a fast, contained failure mode for a slow, whole-process-freezing one.
